title: Bankgesellschaft rejects a merger with CS Holding
what: On the night of 11 April the Bankgesellschaft's board unanimously rejected a merger proposal from CS Holding, whose chairman Rainer Gut had telephoned Nikolaus Senn with the offer. The combined bank would have earned slightly more than 3 billion francs a year and, with a balance sheet of about $419 billion, would have ranked second in the world. A merger could have cost up to 10,000 jobs in Switzerland.
why: The Bankgesellschaft keeps its independence for 20 more months and then merges with the Bankverein on worse terms for its own managers. The share fell 10% in dollars in April.

title: A night guard saves wartime files from the shredder
what: On 8 January Christoph Meili, a security guard at the Bankgesellschaft in Zurich, found employees shredding old records, among them files of the Nazi era, and handed some to a Jewish organisation; the press reported it on 14 January. Shredding such records violates a law passed in December 1996 to protect evidence on wartime assets. Swiss banks are already under pressure from US politicians and Jewish groups over dormant accounts of Holocaust victims.
why: The Meili affair turns the dormant-accounts dispute into Switzerland's biggest foreign-policy crisis since the war and leads to US sanction threats and the $1.25 billion settlement of August 1998. Meili was fired; the big three banks set up a 100-million-franc humanitarian fund in early 1997 (month not confirmed).

title: Bankgesellschaft and Bankverein to merge into UBS
what: On 8 December the Bankgesellschaft and the Bankverein announced an all-stock 'merger of equals' under the name UBS. Bankgesellschaft shareholders get about 60% of the new bank. 13,000 jobs are to go, more than half in Switzerland; the bank targets 10-11 billion francs of profit within four years and would be the world's largest manager of private wealth, with more than 1,000 billion francs of client assets. The Bankverein's Marcel Ospel becomes chief executive, the Bankgesellschaft's Mathis Cabiallavetta chairman. The Bankgesellschaft has recently suffered losses on equity derivatives.
why: The defining beat of the arc: the end of the 'big three' and the birth of UBS. The larger bank gets the majority of the shares, the smaller one the management.

title: UBS is born
what: The merger of the Bankgesellschaft and the Bankverein took legal effect on 27-28 June. The new UBS has total assets of more than $590 billion, making it the second-largest bank in the world. Each Bankverein share becomes 1 1/13 UBS shares and each Bankgesellschaft bearer share five shares of the new bank.
why: Merger beat from the Bankgesellschaft's side: the game's ubs series continues as the new UBS. Six weeks later Russia defaults and LTCM collapses.
source: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schweizerische_Bankgesellschaft (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UBS (read 2026-10-03); share terms: data/src/universe.ts and data/manual/ubs.csv header (read 2026-10-03)

title: UBS caught in the LTCM collapse
what: Long-Term Capital Management's equity fell from $2.3 billion to about $400 million in three weeks. The hedge fund in Greenwich, Connecticut, founded in 1994 by the bond trader John Meriwether, with the Nobel prize winners Myron Scholes and Robert Merton on its board, had borrowed more than $124 billion on top of $4.7 billion of its own money to bet that small price gaps between bonds would close. Russia's default in August set off its losses. On 23 September the New York Fed organised a $3.625 billion rescue by 14 banks, UBS and Credit Suisse among those putting in $300 million each. UBS has its own large exposure through an option deal on LTCM shares struck in 1997. On 30 September UBS shares fell 14% in a day as investors lost confidence in the leadership; an internal investigation is due to report on Friday.
why: The worst month in the ubs series (-40%). UBS was the largest single loser on LTCM (about 950 million francs).
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-Term_Capital_Management (read 2026-10-03); Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 1 October 1998, p. 35 ('Weitere Verluste der UBS-Valoren'), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1998-10-01.pdf (read 2026-10-03); https://www.encyclopedia.com/books/politics-and-business-magazines/ubs-ag (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-Term_Capital_Management (re-read 2026-10-04)

title: UBS takes over PaineWebber
what: UBS completed its takeover of the US broker PaineWebber on 3 November for about $11.8 billion. PaineWebber has 1.9 million mostly affluent clients with $452 billion of assets. It makes UBS a big player in American wealth management.
why: UBS's bet on America: the US wealth business becomes a pillar, but the US presence also exposes the bank to American prosecutors in the tax case of 2008.

title: Chief executive Peter Wuffli steps down
what: On 6 July Peter Wuffli unexpectedly stepped down as chief executive of UBS; Marcel Rohner succeeds him. In May UBS had closed Dillon Read Capital Management, its in-house hedge fund, after losses on US mortgage securities. Markets for such securities are now in turmoil.
why: The first visible sign of the subprime losses that bring UBS to state aid fifteen months later.

title: $10 billion more in write-downs; Singapore steps in
what: On 10 December UBS announced further write-downs of about $10 billion on US subprime mortgage positions and new capital of 13 billion francs: mandatory convertible notes sold to the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation (11 billion) and an investor from the Middle East (2 billion). Shareholders get a stock dividend instead of a cash dividend for 2007. UBS expects a loss for the year.
why: UBS turns to sovereign wealth funds; the 2007 net loss comes to 5.2 billion francs. Its shares fall from 61.95 francs in October to 52.40 at year-end.
source: UBS Form 20-F/A for 2007, filed 14 April 2008, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1114446/000095012308004121/y54449e20vfza.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/UBS (read 2026-10-03)

title: Ospel goes after another $19 billion write-down
what: On 1 April UBS pre-announced a first-quarter net loss of about 12 billion francs on $19 billion of write-downs on US real-estate assets, a fully underwritten rights issue of about 15 billion francs and a separate unit for its bad mortgage positions. Chairman Marcel Ospel is not standing for re-election; the general counsel, Peter Kurer, was elected chairman at the meeting on 23 April. Investors were relieved: the shares rose 15% in dollars in April.
why: End of the Ospel era, which began with the merger in 1998. The relief rally is short-lived.
source: UBS Form 20-F/A for 2007, filed 14 April 2008, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1114446/000095012308004121/y54449e20vfza.htm (read 2026-10-03); UBS Form 20-F for 2008, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1114446/000095012309004436/y75024e20vf.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Rights issue: seven new shares for every twenty
what: UBS shareholders received one free share for every 20 held (record date 25 April, delivered 19 May) instead of a dividend, and then subscription rights for the 15-billion-franc capital increase: for every 20 rights, holders can buy seven new shares at 21 francs. The shares trade ex-rights from the end of May. On 20 May UBS also sold $15 billion of US mortgage securities to a fund run by BlackRock, lending most of the money itself.
why: Part of the -28% is mechanical: the series is not adjusted for the stock dividend or the rights issue (worth very roughly 10% together). The rest is the market's verdict on UBS.

title: The Swiss state rescues UBS
what: On 16 October the Swiss National Bank and the federal government announced measures to strengthen the Swiss financial system. UBS can transfer up to $60 billion of illiquid securities, mostly backed by US home and commercial mortgages, to a fund controlled by the National Bank, which lends it up to $54 billion; UBS puts in up to $6 billion of equity. The Confederation subscribes 6 billion francs of mandatory convertible notes in UBS. Credit Suisse, which raised capital privately, does not use the facility.
why: The defining moment of UBS's crisis. The share barely moved in October (+1%) because the rescue removed the risk of collapse; the state later exits with a profit.
source: Swiss National Bank, media release of 16 October 2008, https://www.snb.ch/public/asset/de/www-snb-ch/publications/communication/press-releases/2008/pre_20081016_1/publications0/pre_20081016_1.de.pdf (read 2026-10-03); UBS Form 20-F for 2008 (read 2026-10-03)

title: UBS settles with the US and hands over client names
what: On 18 February UBS entered a deferred prosecution agreement with the US Department of Justice and pays $780 million; with the backing of the Swiss regulator FINMA it hands over data on a few hundred American clients, breaching the usual reach of bank secrecy. The US tax authorities are separately seeking information on many more accounts. UBS reported a 2008 net loss of 20.9 billion francs, and on 26 February Oswald Grübel replaced Marcel Rohner as chief executive. The shares fell to about 11 francs.
why: The beginning of the end of Swiss bank secrecy for foreign clients, and the low point of UBS's crisis: -86% from the April 2007 peak to March 2009.
source: UBS Form 20-F for 2008, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1114446/000095012309004436/y75024e20vf.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/UBS (read 2026-10-03); prices: data/raw/yahoo/ubs.csv (read 2026-10-03)

title: Grübel cuts costs as markets rebound
what: On 15 April UBS announced cost cuts and set a target of about 65,000 employees for 2010, against about 76,200 at the end of March, and centralised its finance, risk and legal functions. It also agreed to sell its Brazilian unit, UBS Pactual. Share markets kept recovering from their March lows; the S&P 500 gained about 9% in April.
why: The +49% in April is the rebound of a share priced for disaster, helped by the market's turn (S&P 500 +9%).

title: Tax deal with the US; the state cashes in
what: On 19 August UBS settled the US 'John Doe' summons case, and the US and Switzerland signed an agreement under which the IRS asks the Swiss tax administration for information on about 4,450 accounts of American clients. The same day the Confederation announced the conversion of its 6 billion francs of convertible notes into UBS shares.
why: The two great uncertainties of the crisis, the US lawsuit and state ownership, are resolved in one month (+26%). The Confederation sells its shares in the third quarter at a profit of 1.2 billion francs.

title: UBS earns 2 billion francs in a quarter
what: On 27 July UBS reported a net profit of 2,005 million francs for the second quarter of 2010, and outflows of client money from its wealth management continued to ease. The S&P 500 gained about 7% in July.
why: The first convincing proof that UBS is profitable again after the crisis (+27% in dollars, with the franc also firmer).

title: A rogue trader costs UBS $2.3 billion; Grübel resigns
what: On 15 September UBS said unauthorised trading by a trader in London, Kweku Adoboli, had caused a loss estimated at $2 billion, later put at $2.3 billion; the shares fell 10.8% that day. On 24 September chief executive Oswald Grübel resigned; Sergio Ermotti takes over on an interim basis. Earlier in the month, on 6 September, the Swiss National Bank set a minimum exchange rate of 1.20 francs per euro, and the franc fell about 11% against the dollar in September.
why: Ermotti's arrival leads to the 2012 retreat from investment banking. The -20% in dollars is the scandal plus the weaker franc.

title: UBS shrinks its investment bank
what: On 30 October UBS announced it will exit most of its fixed-income trading, keep only advisory, research, equities, currencies and precious metals in the investment bank, and cut costs by another 3.4 billion francs by 2015. The workforce is to fall to about 54,000 from about 64,000. Andrea Orcel takes over the investment bank. UBS aims to pay out 50% or more of profits once its capital plans are met.
why: The strategic turn that makes UBS a wealth manager first; investors loved it (+23% in the month) and it is why UBS, not Credit Suisse, survives to take over its rival in 2023.

title: 1.4 billion francs for Libor manipulation
what: On 19 December UBS agreed to pay about 1.4 billion francs in fines and disgorgement to US, UK and Swiss authorities over attempts to manipulate Libor and other benchmark interest rates; its Japanese securities unit pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud. The settlements push UBS to a loss for 2012.
why: One of the legal bills from the old investment bank; UBS posts a 2012 net loss of 2.5 billion francs despite the strategic turn.

title: The end of bank secrecy for foreign clients
what: From 2017 Switzerland applies the international standard for the automatic exchange of information on bank accounts: Swiss banks collect data on accounts of foreign residents, which will be sent to their home tax authorities from 2018. For depositors who do not live in Switzerland, bank secrecy is effectively over.
why: Closes the bank-secrecy strand that began with the 1984 vote; from 2019 Switzerland shares details of 3.1 million foreign-held accounts.

title: Paris court fines UBS 3.7 billion euros
what: On 20 February a Paris court convicted UBS of illegally soliciting clients in France and laundering the proceeds of tax fraud, and ordered it to pay a record of about 3.7 billion euros, including damages. UBS is appealing.
why: The French case is the long tail of the cross-border business; the appeal court cuts the bill to 1.8 billion euros in December 2021.

title: Credit Suisse becomes part of UBS
what: On 12 June UBS completed the takeover; Credit Suisse Group is now a subsidiary of UBS. Sergio Ermotti, who returned as chief executive in April, has said integrating the two banks will take years. Credit Suisse shareholders received UBS shares.
why: Completion beat from the acquirer's side; the game's credit-suisse holders now own ubs.

title: UBS gives back the state guarantees and books a giant gain
what: On 11 August UBS voluntarily ended the 9-billion-franc loss protection agreement with the Confederation and the public liquidity backstop of the National Bank; Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter said Swiss taxpayers no longer bear any risk. For the second quarter UBS reported provisional negative goodwill of $28.9 billion from buying Credit Suisse so cheaply, and outflows at Credit Suisse have stopped.
why: The market's verdict that UBS got a bargain (+20% in August).

title: Bern wants UBS to hold much more capital
what: In June the Swiss Federal Council proposed tougher rules for systemically important banks, drawing lessons from Credit Suisse: among other things, investments in foreign subsidiaries would have to be fully backed by top-quality capital. On 6 June UBS estimated it would need about $24 billion of additional common equity in its parent bank if the rules were adopted as proposed. Parliament still has to decide.
why: The open question of UBS's arc at the time of writing: how much capital the only remaining Swiss big bank must hold, and whether that limits buybacks or its global ambitions.
